claims.text: Motion sickness in VR (visually induced motion sickness, VIMS) is attributed to a mismatch between visual and vestibular information, causing ambiguity about body position relative to the environment.
An EEG study of 14 healthy subjects in a VR environment found that with increasing visual-vestibular mismatch and subjective VIMS, the proportion of slow EEG waves (especially 1–10 Hz) increases.
Motion sickness is generally evoked from a mismatch in sensory cues between vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive signals integrated in the brainstem and cerebellum.

A study using galvanic vestibular stimulation (GVS) in 10 participants demonstrated that "Beneficial" GVS produced a 26% motion sickness reduction and "Detrimental" GVS produced a 56% increase (p = 0.0055), confirming the causal role of vestibular sensory conflict in motion sickness.

Human studies have found that low-frequency oscillations of 0.2 Hz with large amplitudes are most likely to cause motion sickness, while at frequencies of 2 Hz or above, motion sickness ceases completely.

Vestibular rehabilitation therapy uses personalized exercises targeting eye movements, head movements, and balance retraining to compensate for vestibular dysfunction and reduce motion sickness discomfort.

A clinical study of 30 motion sickness-susceptible participants evaluated fluid-filled glasses (creating an artificial moving horizon) against a placebo group in a computer-assisted rehabilitation environment (CAREN), measuring symptoms with the Motion Sickness Assessment Questionnaire before, after, and at 60-second intervals.
Slow, intermittent exposure to motion and reducing physical, mental, or emotional discomfort are recommended preventive strategies for motion sickness.
Digital environments can accommodate motion sensitivity by limiting parallax scrolling and excessive animations to prevent cybersickness.
The GVS study explicitly states its findings "facilitate new methods and countermeasures for mitigating motion sickness during transportation and in virtual environments."
